title: Slot slicing, hedging and GPU occupancy — platform notes
content:
Purpose
---
Notes exploring a hybrid admission controller that uses fine-grained slot-slicing + hedging to smooth multi-region bursts while keeping GPU occupancy high. Goal: reduce tail latency spikes during region-local bursts without over-provisioning global capacity.

Context / motivation
---
- We've seen repeated short-lived bursts from product features (search preview, chat auto-complete) hitting single regions and saturating specific GPU pools.
- Current token-bucket centric approach is simple but coarse: it throttles request ingress but doesn't preserve per-GPU occupancy efficiently when bursts are short and high-concurrency.
- Need a design that: (a) avoids cold starts/long queueing tails, (b) keeps GPUs near optimal utilization, (c) supports multi-region hedging when local capacity insufficient, and (d) gives predictable SLOs per customer tier.

High-level idea
---
1) Slot-slicing: split each GPU worker's available concurrency into logical "slices" (time-boxed capacity windows). Each slice can be allocated to request cohorts (by customer, route, or latency band). Slices are small (e.g., 50–200ms wall-time windows) so they naturally align with short-token sequences and KV cache reuse.
2) Local token-buckets per-slice: instead of a single bucket per region, maintain multiple thin token-buckets mapped to slices. This reduces head-of-line effects: a short burst consumes only a subset of slices, leaving others available for different cohorts.
3) Queue-depth sentinel + early-drop: per-slice queue depth is tracked and used to trigger early-drop or upstream backpressure before global token exhaustion. This gives fast feedback to clients/degraders.
4) GPU occupancy probe: continuous lightweight sampling of SM/GPU utilization and per-process vram pressure. When occupancy < target but queue depth > 0, we expand slice concurrency temporarily (burst-squeeze). When occupancy >= target and latency rises, we tighten admission.
5) Hedging across regions: when local admission rejects/defers, we send a hedged request to a warm standby region with compatible model variant. Hedging uses a short jitter to avoid amplification; prefer secondary region only when slice-level backlog > threshold or predicted time-to-start > X ms.

Design sketch: slot-slicing model
---
- Worker exposes N logical slices, e.g., N = max_concurrency / k where k is a tuning parameter (k in 4..16). Example: 32-slot slices for an instance with 256 concurrency.
- Each slice has: slice_id, token_bucket(capacity, refill_rate), queue_depth, last_processed_seq_len_stats (for expected processing time).
- Admission: incoming request picks a preferred slice via routing policy: (customer affinity -> slice_affinity) -> pick least-queue slice among allowed. If no slice accepts, attempt hedged routing or return soft-retry.
- Token semantics: tokens represent expected GPU micro-time units (e.g., ms of GPU occupancy) instead of tokens-per-request. This lets us account for request length variability.

Admission control algorithm (pseudocode, informal)
---
1. map request -> preferred_region(s) and slice affinity
2. sample slice candidates (randomized top-k) and read token and queue metrics
3. if any slice has tokens >= est_cost and queue_depth < queue_limit: accept -> decrement tokens -> enqueue
4. else if any slice has tokens < est_cost but GPU occupancy low and backlog small: expand slice temporarily (increase token allowance) and accept
5. else if backlog high and multi-region allowed: initiate hedged request to alternate region (respecting hedging budget and rate limit)
6. else emit soft-reject with retry-after or fallback model

Queue-depth sentinel details
---
- Two levels of queue limit: soft_queue_limit (start early slowdown) and hard_queue_limit (reject). soft limit triggers: route-level re-prioritization, reduce slice token refill, or spawn a quick local fast-path (short-response approximate model).
- Queue depth is maintained per-slice and aggregated to per-worker and per-region signals for telemetry and routing decisions.

GPU occupancy probe and control loop
---
- Probe frequency: 100ms sample heartbeat (low overhead), aggregate into 1s windows for control decisions.
- Control targets: keep occupancy at 65–85% depending on model latency sensitivity and queueing tolerance.
- If occupancy < lower_target and queue_depth>0: allow temporary slice expansion (addXms tokens per slice) for up to M windows.
- If occupancy > upper_target and median latency rising: trigger reject-shed on lowest-priority slices and elevate hedging to alternate pools.

Hedging policy notes
---
- Hedging budget per-customer per-minute to avoid amplification across regions. Default: 2% of requests hedged for SLA customers, 0.1% free tier.
- Warm standby region must be compatible model/quantization and have KV cache warm status; otherwise rollback hedging to queued fallback (approx model).
- Hedging jitter: randomized 8–20ms to avoid synchronized hedging storms. Backoff on observed increased downstream latency.

Metrics and observability (what to emit)
---
- Slice-level: tokens_available, tokens_consumed, queue_depth, avg_processing_ms, rejected_count, early_drops
- Worker-level: slices_active, occupancy_p10/p50/p90, vram_pressure_pct
- Region-level: hedged_request_rate, hedged_success_rate, failover_count, steady-state_latency
- Customer-level: admitted_rate, rejected_rate, hedged_rate, cost_estimate_delta
- Alerts: sustained worker occupancy < 40% with high queue_depth (indicates fragmentation), hedging success_rate < 50% (policy mismatch), sudden increase in early_drops

Tradeoffs / pitfalls
---
- Complexity: slice bookkeeping multiplies state (more RPCs to scheduler). Need careful implementation to avoid per-request latency tax.
- Fairness: slices can lead to inadvertent starvation if affinity rules are aggressive. Must include periodic rebalancing epochs.
- Observability cost: high-cardinality metrics (per-slice) — aggregate to sane rollups and sample heavy slices.
- Hedging amplification: if hedging not budgeted, it can double work. Enforce strict global hedging caps.

Rollout plan (phased)
---
1) Simulation: run synthetic traces (spike profiles from product via INF-logs) through slice model, validate occupancy and latency improvements.
2) Canary: implement on low-traffic region + non-critical routes (embeddings or background rerank) for 2 weeks.
3) Measure: key metrics (p99 latency, GPU occupancy, hedging cost). Validate no net increase in tail-cost ratio > 1.05 for normal traffic.
4) Gradual expansion: enable for more regions and select customer tiers; provide toggle per-customer via console.

Operational playbook highlights
---
- If early_drops spike in multiple regions -> rollback hedging toggles and inspect queue-depth distribution + top request shapes.
- If occupancy low but queues persist -> investigate fragmentation; run slice rebalance job and consider merging slices temporarily.
- If hedging cost exceeds budget -> tighten hedging budget and enable local soft-fallback models.

Open questions / TODOs
---
- Estimate CPU/coordination overhead for slice management at 1M qps global. Need microbenchmark. (@Liam)
- Determine k (slice granularity) sweet spot via A/B (4, 8, 16) and correlate with KV-cache hit rates. (@Marta)
- Explore hybrid tokens: time-based tokens + memory-based tokens to reflect VRAM pressure.
- Integrate with existing token-bucket code paths (compat layer) vs rewrite. Fast path compatibility is critical.

References / related tickets
---
- INF-4567 experimental traces used for synthetic testing
- Linear: RED-1234 slot-slicing spike experiment board
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/ingress/pull/987 (entrypoint hooks for hedging)

Notes-to-self
---
- Keep slices small initially to minimize state and observe benefits. If we see high coordination overhead, fallback to a two-tier approach (regional buckets + worker micro-buckets with TTL).
- Add a "slice-rebalance" cron job that runs every 5m to avoid persistent fragmentation.

End of notes (sketch)
